_help: Fish the Dead Projects: the catches. Real projects that died, each with what it promised, its peak (a figure only where well documented, otherwise in words), why it died (what went wrong, never how), the year it died, rarity (1 common, 2 rare, 3 legendary: bigger collapses are rarer and score more) and sources. Entries with fresh: true are the 2026 shutdowns from the CoinStats tracker: they only have a name and date so far (promised and peak are empty and hidden until filled in), weight (0.15) makes each one bite less often so the classic catches still turn up, and their source has no link yet (add the article address in url). date (2026 entries) puts them in order on the shark dive. Every entry is marked review: true until you have checked it against its sources; then set it to false.

catches.name: Terra (LUNA)
catches.promised: A blockchain for payments, powering its own dollar stablecoin.
catches.died: When its stablecoin lost its dollar peg, LUNA was printed in huge amounts and fell more than 99% in days.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Terra

catches.name: TerraUSD (UST)
catches.promised: A digital dollar kept at $1 by code instead of cash in a bank.
catches.died: Big withdrawals broke the $1 peg in May 2022, and confidence never came back.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Terra

catches.name: FTX Token (FTT)
catches.promised: Discounts and perks on FTX, one of the biggest exchanges.
catches.died: FTX collapsed in November 2022 after customer money was found missing; its founder was later convicted of fraud.

sources.label: Wikipedia: FTX

catches.name: Celsius (CEL)
catches.promised: High interest on your crypto, with a bank-like feel.
catches.peak: Billions of dollars in customer deposits (2021).
catches.died: It froze withdrawals in June 2022 and went bankrupt; its founder later pleaded guilty to fraud.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Celsius Network

catches.name: OneCoin
catches.promised: The next Bitcoin, sold through education packages.
catches.peak: More than $4 billion raised from investors (2014 to 2016).
catches.died: There was never a real blockchain; its founder vanished in 2017 and is still wanted.

sources.label: Wikipedia: OneCoin

catches.name: Diem (Libra)
catches.promised: A global digital currency from Facebook for billions of users.
catches.peak: Backed by Facebook and big partners at launch (2019).
catches.died: Regulators pushed back for years, and the project was sold off and shut in 2022.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Diem

catches.name: BitConnect (BCC)
catches.promised: Daily profits from a secret trading bot.
catches.died: Regulators ordered it to stop in January 2018 and the price crashed; US authorities called it a Ponzi scheme.

sources.label: Wikipedia: BitConnect

catches.name: SafeMoon
catches.promised: A token that rewards holders and goes "safely to the moon".
catches.peak: Billions of dollars in market value (2021).
catches.died: The company went bankrupt in 2023 and US prosecutors charged its leaders with fraud.

sources.label: Wikipedia: SafeMoon

catches.name: Iron Finance (TITAN)
catches.promised: A partly backed stablecoin with sky-high yields.
catches.died: A run on the stablecoin in June 2021 sent TITAN to almost zero within a day.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Iron Finance

catches.name: Wonderland (TIME)
catches.promised: Huge yields from a shared treasury.
catches.died: In January 2022 its treasury manager was revealed to be a co-founder of a collapsed exchange, and trust vanished.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Wonderland

catches.name: QuadrigaCX
catches.promised: Canada's easy place to buy bitcoin.
catches.peak: Customers owed about C$215 million when it failed (2019).
catches.died: After its founder died in 2018, most customer money turned out to be missing.

sources.label: Wikipedia: QuadrigaCX

catches.name: The DAO
catches.promised: An investment fund run by its token holders, with no managers.
catches.died: A bug let an attacker drain a third of it; Ethereum rolled back the theft and the project shut down.

sources.label: Wikipedia: The DAO

catches.name: Fei Protocol
catches.promised: A new kind of stablecoin, launched with huge demand.
catches.died: After years of struggle and a big hack at a partner, the team wound it down in 2022.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Fei Protocol

catches.name: Basis
catches.promised: A stablecoin run purely by code.
catches.died: US securities rules made the design unworkable, and it returned money and shut down in 2018.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Basis

catches.name: Squid Game token
catches.promised: A play-to-earn game riding a hit TV show.
catches.died: Buyers could not sell, and the creators cashed out and vanished the same day.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Squid Game token

catches.name: AnubisDAO
catches.promised: A new dog-themed DeFi project.
catches.peak: About $60 million raised in a day (October 2021).
catches.died: The money left its wallet within a day of the sale and was never returned.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rug pull

catches.name: Frosties NFT
catches.promised: Cute ice cream NFTs with games and rewards to come.
catches.died: The creators shut the site and kept the money; they were later charged in the US.

sources.label: US Attorney, SDNY

catches.name: PlexCoin
catches.promised: Returns of more than 1,000% in about a month.
catches.died: US regulators froze it in December 2017 as a fraud.

sources.label: SEC press release

catches.name: Centra Tech
catches.promised: A crypto debit card backed by big banks, promoted by celebrities.
catches.died: The bank partnerships were fake; its founders were charged in 2018 and later convicted.

sources.label: SEC press release

catches.name: Bitcoin Savings and Trust
catches.promised: 7% interest a week on bitcoin.
catches.peak: At least 700,000 bitcoin taken in (2011 to 2012).
catches.died: It paid old investors with new deposits until it collapsed in 2012.

sources.label: SEC press release
